name: SlimFast diet

lead: The SlimFast diet replaces breakfast and lunch with a branded shake or bar and leaves one ordinary low-calorie dinner. By lowering daily calories in a simple, portion-controlled way, it is used to lose fat, which makes the face look leaner and the jaw and cheekbones more defined.

The product line launched in the United States in 1977. Randomized trials, including a UK trial of 300 adults, found weight losses of roughly 5 to 9 kg over six months with the SlimFast plan, similar to other commercial diets compared in the same study.

paras: Users swap two daily meals for a shake or bar, eat a calorie-controlled dinner and snacks, and track weight. The plan is often used as a short cut for a weight-loss phase rather than as a permanent routine, and some pair it with strength training to keep muscle.

Reported issues are mainly practical: hunger, monotony and regaining weight when the plan ends. People with diabetes were studied with sugar-free versions under supervision. Product recalls have occurred, including a 2009 recall of canned products over possible bacterial contamination.

chain: Replace two meals with a shake or bar
angle.text: The plan lowers calorie intake with ready-made, portion-controlled meals. Fat loss makes facial structure and body definition more visible, which is how dieters use it for appearance.

lead: SlimFast is a brand of shakes, bars and snacks, and the diet built around them: two meals a day are replaced by SlimFast products and one regular meal, usually dinner, is kept low in calories.[1] People looking to look leaner use it as a structured way to cut calories, since less body fat tends to sharpen the jawline, cheeks and overall definition.

The brand began as a line from Thompson Medical Company, founded by S. Daniel Abraham, which rolled it out nationally on July 11, 1977 as a protein supplement.[1] Ownership later passed to Unilever (2000), Kainos Capital (2014) and Glanbia (2018), and in September 2025 the US brand was acquired by Heartland Food Products Group.[1]

Several randomized trials have included SlimFast as an arm or as the intervention. A UK trial of 300 overweight adults over six months found weight losses of 5 to 9 kg across four commercial diets including SlimFast, with no significant difference between them.[2]

paras: In its original form (1987 to 2004), SlimFast was a line of chocolate, strawberry and vanilla shakes meant to replace breakfast and lunch, with a self-chosen low-calorie dinner; meal bars were added in the mid-1990s.[1] The company now also sells snacks and packaged meals.[1]

Thompson Medical, which also sold the supplement Dexatrim, launched SlimFast as a product line in 1977; S. Daniel Abraham took the brand private in 1987.[1] Unilever acquired it in 2000 and sold it to Kainos Capital in 2014; Glanbia bought it in 2018, and Heartland acquired the US brand in September 2025, with UK and European operations sold to Supreme the following month.[1] In 2009 the company recalled its canned products over possible bacterial contamination and moved to plastic bottles in 2011.[1]

A 2015 systematic review in the Annals of Internal Medicine evaluated commercial weight-loss programs; Wikipedia summarizes the evidence on SlimFast as mixed and similar to behavioral counseling.[3][1]

The BBC 'diet trials' randomized controlled trial in the UK compared four commercial programs including Slim-Fast, and its lipid analysis reported 5 to 9 kg weight loss over six months in all dieting groups, without significant differences between them.[4][5]

Earlier work looked at the product as a minimal-intervention plan: in a 1994 study of 301 adults given Ultra Slim-Fast with only its package insert, 91% completed 12 weeks.[6] A 2001 randomized trial in 75 adults with type 2 diabetes tested sugar-free Slim-Fast against an exchange diet over 12 weeks.[7] Trials of meal replacements more broadly include a 2011 randomized trial in adolescents and a 2004 comparison with a structured diet in adults with metabolic syndrome features.[8][9]

Human trials exist. A multicentre UK randomized trial of 300 adults compared the Slim-Fast plan with Atkins, Weight Watchers, Rosemary Conley and a control diet over six months, finding weight loss of 5 to 9 kg in all dieting groups and no significant differences between diets.[5] A 1994 trial reported 91% of 301 participants completing 12 weeks of a minimal-intervention plan.[6] A 2001 randomized trial of 75 adults with type 2 diabetes tested sugar-free Slim-Fast.[7] Systematic reviews of commercial programs have also pooled these trials.[3]
